synopsis: Automatic braking can itself destabilize heavy off-road machines through load shift, rollover, sliding, articulation effects and secondary collisions, particularly on slopes, with elevated or suspended loads, or during manoeuvres [f117, f5814, f5941]. Komatsu requires KomVision to be off during trailer loading; its wheel-loader guidance also calls for disabling stop control on slopes, slippery or soft ground and with suspended loads, on an undated page accessed in 2026 [f1646, f10550]. The booklet’s published position is to cap commanded deceleration at the minimum of collision-avoidance need, traction, stability, machine braking capability and load limits, while limiting jerk to reduce operator jolts and load shift [f11888, f13638]. Validation therefore needs loading and implement-position coverage, controllability outcomes beyond stopping distance, and richer models where articulation, high centres of gravity or deformable terrain matter [f3400, f6149, f6075, f6077]. These hazards are mechanically credible, but quantified off-road load-shift incidents and direct evidence of automatic-braking-induced rollover or slope instability were not found; shadow mode cannot establish actual stopping stability or load movement [f3397, f3405, f595, f597].
